title: Hammer vs feather

scenes.text: A hammer and a feather. Which lands first?
On Earth, the hammer wins easily.
So heavier things fall faster, right?

visual.sub: Aristotle's idea, taught for nearly 2,000 years

scenes.text: Nope. The feather isn't losing to gravity. It's losing to the AIR.
1971: on the airless Moon, astronaut David Scott tried it.
They landed at the same time.
Without air, everything falls with the same acceleration, whatever its mass.

visual.sub: ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth  ·  ≈ 1.6 m/s² on the Moon

scenes.text: Follow for daily physics. Now, on Earth: a hammer and a feather…

upload.title: Hammer vs Feather on the Moon: Which Lands First? #physics #shorts
upload.description: On Earth the hammer wins, but not because it's heavier. Air resistance slows the light, wide feather. In 1971 Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon, with no air, and they hit the ground together. In a vacuum, objects at the same place fall with the same acceleration, whatever their mass (about 9.8 m/s² on Earth, 1.6 m/s² on the Moon).
upload.pinned_comment: Before you watched: hammer or feather? Be honest 👇

sources: NASA SP-289, Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (hammer 1.32 kg, falcon feather 0.03 kg, dropped from about 1.6 m)
